extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, graduate students, and mathematically-interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a claimed mathematical proof is correct, credible, and accepted by the research community (illustrated by the Mochizuki abc controversy). Focuses on understandability, peer review, community vetting, and editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof validity (a proof is either valid or not)
rubrics_metrics.description: "After all, an argument is either a valid proof, or it is not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes that correctness is the fundamental standard: a proof must be logically correct. However, the narrative also notes practical complications (see understandability and verifiability) — a proof can be correct in principle yet remain unaccepted if the community cannot verify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understandability and verifiability by the community
rubrics_metrics.description: The community must be able to understand substantial parts of a work in order to corroborate or discard the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post recounts that "most of the mathematical community... was simply unable to understand the work, not even in some substantial part, which could have helped to corroborate or discard the results." It implies that a proof should be presented at a level that allows independent experts to follow and check the arguments (exposition, examples, decomposition into checkable pieces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of concrete examples and illustrative instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide interesting examples to accompany abstract constructions (Brian Conrad's metaphor about being told to "Consider a pair of isomorphic vector spaces" but never given an interesting example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog quotes Conrad to highlight that abstract claims without illustrative examples hinder understanding — effective proofs/theories should include examples that illuminate the constructions and claims, especially when new abstract concepts are introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent, independent peer review and journal endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in an established, independently operated, peer-reviewed journal increases credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes the absence of journal acceptance as a credibility problem and discusses the unusual circumstances of eventual publication in Publ. RIMS. It implies that independent peer review and endorsement by journals with no conflicts is an important criterion for accepting major claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of conflicts of interest in editorial processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial independence is essential; conflicts (e.g., author holding editorial authority at the publishing journal) damage credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that the sponsoring institute (RIMS) and the author were closely tied and that Mochizuki was editor-in-chief of the journal that published his papers; this, together with claims about the author being unaware of the review process, "permanently damaged" credibility. Guidance: avoid editorial situations that create perceived or real conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community vetting via workshops/conferences and expert discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Organised community events (workshops, focused conferences) and participation by experts are a route to understanding and validating difficult work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Clay Institute/Oxford 2015 conference and the 2018 visit by Scholze and Stix are cited as mechanisms intended to sift the work through the community. The post shows that such events are useful but not sufficient if the work remains opaque — they should be structured to produce concrete, checkable progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement and cooperation from the author (accessibility of the author)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should cooperate in facilitating understanding of their work (expository talks, travel, interaction), not only by posting preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mochizuki "was willing to cooperate... — as long as he did it from Kyoto, refusing to leave his residence." The narrative implies that limited engagement hinders community verification; more active, accessible participation aids understanding and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit statement of foundational assumptions and set-theoretic bases
rubrics_metrics.description: New large theories should clearly state foundational and set-theoretic assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of Mochizuki's IUTT parts is titled "Log-volume Computations and Set-theoretic Foundations," reflecting that novel theories must clarify foundational framework so others can verify correctness and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use and compatibility with recent/known results
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments must correctly employ and be compatible with recent results in the field; misuse can create gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post recounts that Scholze and Stix identified an "argument gap" tied to a very recent result in Arithmetic Geometry (itself due to Mochizuki), showing that reliance on or interaction with recent work must be carefully justified and checked to avoid circularity or misapplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary consequences demand especially clear derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theory claims to prove many famous results (e.g., abc => Roth, Faltings, Fermat's Last Theorem), the derivations must be especially transparent and checkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because IUTT purportedly implied many major theorems, the community expected clearer, verifiable derivations; when claims have wide-reaching consequences, scrutiny and clarity requirements are heightened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints as provisional communications requiring further review
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints announce results but are "not yet duly corrected and reviewed by expert researchers" and so require careful follow-up and community verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mochizuki's 2012 preprints were circulated but not published; the post treats preprints as a first step whose claims become credible only after thorough expert checking and, ideally, journal peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, development of tools, and persistence may be needed for resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding and community acceptance of difficult work can take years and may depend on future development of tools and exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post suggests that "in a few years' time, the tools needed to better understand the IUTT's approach will probably be more readily available," indicating that temporal persistence and subsequent clarifications can be legitimate paths to eventual acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility and professional tone in scholarly debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly disagreements should be conducted civilly; aggressive or uncivil exchanges hinder productive assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article mentions unusually aggressive rebuttals and uncivil discussion (e.g., blog debates on Not Even Wrong), implying that respectful discourse is an implicit standard for effective community vetting.
